prompt: Which subatomic particle has a positive charge?
explanation: Protons are positively charged and live in the nucleus. Electrons are negative; neutrons are neutral (no charge); photons aren't even part of the atom — they're particles of light. The number of protons defines what element you have.

prompt: An element with 6 protons is which element? (Answer with the name.)
explanation: Atomic number = number of protons. Atomic number 6 = carbon. The number of protons defines the element completely — change it and you've changed elements. Carbon's six protons are why it sits at position 6 on the periodic table.

prompt: Two atoms are isotopes if they have:
options: Different total mass with same proton+neutron count
explanation: Isotopes are variants of the same element (so same proton count) with different neutron counts. Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 both have 6 protons but 6 vs 8 neutrons. Different protons would mean different elements entirely. Isotopes have similar chemistry but different masses and stability.

prompt: Why are noble gases so unreactive?
options: Their outer electron shells are already full
correctAnswer: Their outer electron shells are already full
explanation: Atoms generally 'want' full outer shells. Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar...) already have them, so they have no chemical drive to gain, lose, or share electrons. This is why helium balloons don't react and neon signs don't catch fire. Reactive elements are those one or two electrons away from a full shell.

prompt: Match each particle to its property:
explanation: These three particles plus the rules of electron shells explain virtually all of chemistry. The nucleus (protons + neutrons) provides identity and most of the mass; electrons in the outer shell drive chemical behavior.

prompt: In an ionic bond, atoms:
options: Transfer electrons from one to another
correctAnswer: Transfer electrons from one to another
explanation: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer — one atom donates, another receives. The donor becomes positively charged, the receiver negatively charged, and opposite charges attract. Sharing is what covalent bonds do. Nuclei never combine in chemistry — that's nuclear physics.

prompt: Water (H₂O) is held together by which type of bond?
explanation: In water, oxygen shares electrons with each hydrogen — it's a covalent compound. (Hydrogen bonds DO exist between water molecules, but those are weaker intermolecular attractions, not the bond holding H₂O itself together.) Covalent bonds dominate the chemistry of life.

prompt: Why can metals conduct electricity?
options: Free-moving electrons in the metallic bond carry current
correctAnswer: Free-moving electrons in the metallic bond carry current
explanation: Metallic bonding pools outer electrons into a 'sea' that flows freely between metal ions. When you apply voltage, those electrons drift — that's electric current. Salt crystals (ionic) don't conduct as solids because their electrons are locked in place; they only conduct when dissolved.

prompt: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is held together by which kind of bond? (one word)
explanation: Sodium gives up its 1 outer electron; chlorine takes it. The resulting Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions attract — a classic ionic bond. NaCl forms a crystal lattice, dissolves well in water, and conducts electricity when dissolved (as the ions separate).

prompt: Match each bond type to its key feature:

pairs.right: Sea of free electrons among metal ions

explanation: These three bond types account for nearly all chemistry. Ionic = transfer, covalent = share, metallic = pool. Each produces materials with characteristic properties: brittle crystals, discrete molecules, conductive shiny solids respectively.

prompt: Elements in the same GROUP (column) of the periodic table share:
options: The same number of outer-shell electrons
correctAnswer: The same number of outer-shell electrons
explanation: Outer electrons drive chemistry, so elements in the same group behave similarly. Group 1 (alkali metals) all have 1 outer electron and react violently with water. Group 18 (noble gases) all have full outer shells and barely react. Geography reveals chemistry.

prompt: Which element is the most electronegative?
explanation: Fluorine, top right of the table (excluding noble gases), pulls electrons hardest. The trend: electronegativity increases up and to the right. Fluorine's combination of small atomic radius and 7 outer electrons makes it the elemental electron-grabbing champion.

prompt: Atomic radius generally:
options: Increases across a period (left to right)
Decreases across a period and increases down a group
correctAnswer: Decreases across a period and increases down a group
explanation: Down a group: each new period adds an electron shell, so atoms get bigger. Across a period: more protons in the nucleus pull the same shell of electrons inward, shrinking the atom. So atoms grow downward and shrink rightward.

prompt: Mendeleev's periodic table was remarkable because it:
options: Predicted the existence and properties of elements not yet discovered
Was the first table ever made
Used atomic numbers (which weren't known yet)
correctAnswer: Predicted the existence and properties of elements not yet discovered
explanation: Mendeleev (1869) noticed gaps in his pattern and predicted missing elements with specific properties — gallium and germanium were later discovered matching his predictions. Predictive power separates real theories from mere classifications. He worked with atomic weight; modern tables use atomic number.

prompt: Match each periodic trend to its direction:
explanation: These three trends are inverses or correlates. Smaller atoms (top right) hold electrons more tightly: high electronegativity, high ionization energy. Larger atoms (bottom left) lose electrons easily and don't grab onto new ones strongly. The patterns are not arbitrary — they follow from atomic structure.

prompt: What law requires that chemical equations be balanced?
explanation: Atoms aren't created or destroyed in chemical reactions, only rearranged. So the same atom counts must appear on both sides — that's a balanced equation. (Energy conservation is also true but addresses energy flow, not mass balance.)

prompt: Balance: __ H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. What coefficient goes before H₂?
explanation: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. Right side has 4 H and 2 O. Left side needs 4 H (from 2 H₂) and 2 O (from O₂). Balanced. The hydrogen-oxygen reaction is highly exothermic and powers rocket engines.

prompt: A reaction A + B → AB is what type?
explanation: Synthesis reactions combine two or more reactants into a single product. Decomposition is the reverse (AB → A + B). The pattern of reactants vs products tells you the reaction type, which helps predict products you haven't seen before.

prompt: An exothermic reaction:
explanation: Exo = out, thermic = heat. Exothermic reactions release energy, usually as heat. Combustion, freezing, and neutralization are exothermic. Endothermic reactions (cold packs, melting, photosynthesis) absorb heat and feel cold to the touch.

prompt: Match each reaction type to its general form:
explanation: Recognizing reaction types lets you predict products and balance equations more efficiently. Most everyday chemistry — cooking, burning, rusting, digesting — falls into these patterns. Combustion alone underwrites most of human energy use.

prompt: In the Brønsted–Lowry definition, an acid is:
explanation: Brønsted–Lowry: acids donate H⁺ (protons); bases accept them. HCl gives up its proton in water (HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻), so it's an acid. This definition cleanly handles chemistry beyond just water solutions, where the older 'OH⁻ producer' definition struggles.

prompt: What pH value is neutral?
explanation: Pure water at 25°C has pH 7. Below 7 is acidic (more H⁺); above 7 is basic (more OH⁻). The scale is logarithmic — pH 4 has 1000× more H⁺ than pH 7. Neutral isn't 'no H⁺' — it's equal H⁺ and OH⁻.

prompt: How much more acidic is pH 3 than pH 5?
explanation: pH is logarithmic — each unit is 10×. Two units = 100× more H⁺. pH 3 has 100× more hydrogen ions than pH 5. This logarithmic compression is why small pH differences in your blood (7.35 vs 7.45) actually mean substantial concentration changes.

prompt: When HCl meets NaOH, they:
explanation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. H⁺ from acid pairs with OH⁻ from base to form water; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ remain as table salt. This is why antacids work — the base neutralizes excess stomach acid, producing harmless salt and water.

prompt: Match each substance to its approximate pH:
explanation: These pH benchmarks give intuition for the scale. Most foods are mildly acidic (pH 2–6); most cleaning products are basic (pH 8–13); biological fluids hover near neutral. Strong acids and strong bases are both dangerous because they aggressively react with biological molecules.

prompt: What is the main shortcoming of Bohr's atomic model?
options: It treats electrons as point particles in fixed orbits, failing for any multi-electron atom
correctAnswer: It treats electrons as point particles in fixed orbits, failing for any multi-electron atom
explanation: Bohr explained hydrogen's spectrum but not helium's. Electrons aren't point particles in orbits — they are quantum waves with probability distributions, described by the Schrödinger equation.

prompt: Atomic orbitals are:
options: 3D probability distributions for an electron's location
correctAnswer: 3D probability distributions for an electron's location
explanation: An orbital is |ψ|² — the probability density for finding the electron at each point. The shapes (s spherical, p dumbbell, d cloverleaf...) reflect this density.

prompt: How many quantum numbers fully specify an electron's state in an atom?
explanation: n (principal), l (angular momentum), m_l (magnetic), m_s (spin). The Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons in the same atom share all four. This sets the structure of the periodic table.

prompt: The 4s orbital fills before 3d in most neutral transition-metal atoms.
explanation: 4s is slightly lower in energy than 3d for neutral atoms (though the gap is small and reversed in some ions). This is the rule that makes Sc through Zn 'transition metals' filling 3d while having 4s² already.

prompt: Match each quantum number to what it describes:

pairs.right: Angular momentum — shape (s, p, d, f)

explanation: Together these four numbers fully specify an electronic state. The structure of the periodic table follows directly from filling rules over these quantum numbers.

prompt: Going across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally:
options: Decreases (rising effective nuclear charge pulls electrons in)
correctAnswer: Decreases (rising effective nuclear charge pulls electrons in)
explanation: Adding protons within the same shell increases Z_eff, contracting the electron cloud. Across period 2: Li (152 pm) → Ne (38 pm) — about a 4× decrease.

prompt: Why does fluorine have such a high electronegativity?
options: Small radius + high effective nuclear charge → strong pull on bonding electrons
correctAnswer: Small radius + high effective nuclear charge → strong pull on bonding electrons
explanation: Pauling electronegativity 3.98 — the highest. The combination of small size (close approach to bonded atom) and high Z_eff (strong attraction) pulls bonding electrons strongly toward F.

prompt: The lanthanide contraction explains why:
options: 5d transition metals are about the same size as 4d ones, leading to dense and similar-chemistry pairs (Nb/Ta, Mo/W)
correctAnswer: 5d transition metals are about the same size as 4d ones, leading to dense and similar-chemistry pairs (Nb/Ta, Mo/W)
explanation: Poor 4f screening makes 5d/6s electrons feel a strong Z_eff and contract sharply across the lanthanides. By the time you reach Hf, it's about the same size as Zr — and chemistry is so similar they're hard to separate.

prompt: Gold's yellow color comes from relativistic effects on the 5d-6s gap.
explanation: Relativistic contraction of 6s and stabilization of 5d narrows the gap into the blue/violet range. Gold absorbs blue light and reflects yellow. Silver, with a wider gap, reflects all visible light — and looks silver.

prompt: Match the trend going LEFT-to-RIGHT across a period:
explanation: These trends correlate because they all derive from rising Z_eff. They're robust enough to make qualitative predictions about new elements before measurement.

prompt: In a redox reaction:
options: One species loses (oxidized) and another gains (reduced)
correctAnswer: One species loses (oxidized) and another gains (reduced)
explanation: Oxidation and reduction always occur together — there's no source of electrons that doesn't have a sink. OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss; Reduction Is Gain.

prompt: What is the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO₄?
explanation: K is +1, each O is -2 (×4 = -8). Total = 0 → Mn must be +7. Permanganate (MnO₄⁻) is a powerful oxidant; the very high oxidation state of Mn makes it eager to gain electrons.

prompt: A galvanic cell with E_cell° = +1.10 V (Cu²⁺/Cu cathode, Zn²⁺/Zn anode) is:
explanation: Positive E_cell° → negative ΔG° → spontaneous. ΔG° = -nFE° = -2 × 96485 × 1.10 ≈ -212 kJ/mol. The classic Cu/Zn battery (Daniell cell) demonstrates this.

prompt: Galvanizing protects iron because zinc is more readily oxidized than iron.
explanation: Zn² (E° = -0.76 V) is more reducing than Fe (-0.44 V). Even when scratched, the exposed zinc corrodes preferentially, sparing the iron underneath. 'Sacrificial' protection is also why ships have zinc anodes attached to their hulls.

prompt: Match each redox process to its example:

pairs.right: CO₂ + H₂O → glucose + O₂ (driven by light)
Zn coating sacrificially oxidizes to protect Fe

explanation: Energy production (food, fuel, batteries) and corrosion are dominated by redox chemistry. The same conceptual framework applies across all of them.
